profiles.name: Egbert Aswell Trumble
profiles.description: Egbert Aswell Trumble was a Rains County, Texas farmer, an official of the Farmers and Laborers Protective Association, a Socialist Party election official and the Socialist candidate for Rains County sheriff in 1904. He spoke at the first of the anti-draft meetings held in the county in the summer of 1917, called after local farmers complained that their draft quota was unfairly high; at a meeting on July 29 participants allegedly voted that draft-age men should resist induction and that older residents should help them. Rumours that the farmers meant to burn the town of Emory, form armed camps and attack officials proved baseless — no town was attacked, no encampment or arms cache was found, and the defendants did not resist arrest — but about fifty people were seized in raids beginning on the night of August 8, 1917. He was among the forty-six released on individual $2,000 bonds. Tried at Tyler from September 9, 1918 in a trial lasting some ten days, he was one of twenty-three convicted, of federal seditious conspiracy connected to resistance to the Selective Service Act, and sentenced to two years alongside his son John and John O’Rear. The Fifth Circuit affirmed on November 25, 1919, holding that abandoning the planned resistance did not erase criminal responsibility once the conspiracy had formed. He entered USP Atlanta on January 31, 1920 and was paroled on December 4, 1920. His brother Joe and his son John were imprisoned with him.

profiles.name: Henry William Watts
profiles.description:
Henry William Watts was an immigrant who arrived in the United States in 1914.

Journalist. Migrated to US from Canada in 1914. Immediately joined the Socialist Party of America in Everett, Washington. January 1915 began writing for the Washington Socialist; February 1915 became its business manager. Continued that role for the paper’s successor, the Northwest Worker, of which he became editor in April 1916. He wrote in support of the IWW and of “collective ownership” (by workers) rather than “state socialism” (i.e. government ownership). Arrested August 1916 for protesting police repression of IWW speakers in Everett. Arrested again April 6, 1917 for libel of local military recruiters; charges dismissed. Arrested once more October 25, 1917 as an alien “anarchist”; released on bail after seven weeks. While in jail, continued as editor of the Northwest Worker and its successor, The Co-operative News. Eventually deported solely on the dubious grounds that he had been “likely to become a public charge” at the time of his entry into the US. Deported to Canada, February 27, 1918–making him the first known deportee of the Red Scare.

INS file 54235/57 (file missing); FBI file OG 52458

See also: https://depts.washington.edu/labhist/laborpress/NWWorker.htm; https://depts.washington.edu/labhist/laborpress/CoopNews.htm; The Co-operative News, February 21 and February 28, 1918

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Joe Trumble
profiles.description: Joe Trumble was a Rains County, Texas farmer, brother of E. A. Trumble and uncle of John William Trumble, convicted with them at Tyler in September 1918 of federal seditious conspiracy connected to resistance to the Selective Service Act. The case grew out of anti-draft meetings held in the county in the summer of 1917 after local farmers complained their draft quota was unfairly high; rumours of a planned uprising proved baseless, but about fifty people were seized in raids beginning on the night of August 8, 1917. He received the lightest of the family sentences, one year and one day, remained at liberty through the appeal, and entered USP Atlanta on January 31, 1920 as prisoner 10613. His sentence was commuted on October 13, 1920 and he was released a week later, on October 20. He was granted a full presidential pardon on June 19, 1923. The National Archives prisoner index appears to misspell his surname as Trunble.

profiles.name: John William Trumble
profiles.description: John William Trumble was born on September 24, 1888 at Point in Rains County, Texas, the son of E. A. Trumble, and was a member of the Farmers and Laborers Protective Association identified in contemporary political-prisoner material as a Socialist. At the larger of the two anti-draft meetings held in the county in the summer of 1917 — called after local farmers complained their draft quota was unfairly high — he reportedly led a smaller group away from the main assembly to continue discussing resistance to induction. Rumours that the farmers meant to burn the town of Emory, form armed camps and attack officials proved baseless, but about fifty people were seized in raids beginning on the night of August 8, 1917; he was among the forty-six released on individual $2,000 bonds. Tried at Tyler from September 9, 1918, he was one of twenty-three convicted, of federal seditious conspiracy connected to resistance to the Selective Service Act, and was sentenced to two years alongside his father and John O’Rear. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the convictions on November 25, 1919. He entered USP Atlanta on January 31, 1920 and was paroled on December 4, 1920. He died on May 7, 1952 in Lampasas County, Texas.

profiles.name: Karl Malmstrom
profiles.description:
Karl Malmstrom was born 1897 in Ystad, Sweden. Immigrated to the United States in 1915.

Joined the IWW in Portland, Oregon, December 1916. Arrested February 1917 in San Francisco for distributing IWW literature and sentenced to sixty days, he was arrested again in Seattle in 1918 on the same charge and in Everett, Washington, March 1919, when he was held for deportation. Asked if he wished to become a US citizen, he replied, “Never…I am a citizen of the world,” and stated “that workers should be ready to take up arms for industrial freedom”For the workers to get industrial freedom, I would pick up arms at any time…Just like in Russia—do away with the parasites.” He was deported June 29, 1919 as “likely to become a public charge.”

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: LeRoy Nathaniel Bundy
profiles.description: LeRoy Nathaniel Bundy was a dentist and the principal Black political organizer in East St. Louis, Illinois at the time of the July 2, 1917 race massacre. The state authorities, declining to prosecute most white attackers, charged Bundy with conspiring to lead a Black "mob" that allegedly sparked the riot. Convicted March 28, 1919 in Waterloo, Illinois on testimony from Edward Wilson who himself admitted Bundy had not participated; sentenced to life imprisonment. Served one year, working as a dentist inside the prison, before the Illinois Supreme Court reversed his conviction (one juror declared insane; coercion of witnesses; insufficient evidence). Moved to Cleveland, earned law degree at Western Reserve, became prominent UNIA leader.

profiles.name: Louis Lavine
profiles.description: Louis Lavine was an IWW member arrested near Hornbrook, California in early 1917. A March 1917 IWW account titled "The Case of Louis Lavine" describes him riding a freight train when railroad brakemen ordered him to jump at about twenty miles an hour; when they tried to force him off, Lavine reportedly displayed a pair of pliers in a manner meant to resemble a handgun. He was arrested at Hornbrook on an accusation described as shooting at a person with intent to kill — although the object he displayed was not a firearm. The formal charge as filed has not been found. A later IWW item, spelling the surname Lavie, reported him due for release on June 26, 1917; the matching circumstances and chronology make it highly probable the two names are one prisoner. The projected release is recorded in this text only — an expected date is not a documented release, so none is entered on the case.

profiles.name: Morris Becker
profiles.description:
Morris Becker was an anarchist and a vegetarian from New York, New York. Morris Becker was sentenced to a year and eight months in prison. He served in Atlanta Penitentiary from June 19, 1917, to July 25, 1917, and from September 12, 1917, to December 27, 1918. Becker was deported after being rearrested in December 1918 for failing to register for the draft.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Supporter of Alexander Berkman’s The Blast and participated in the No-Conscription League. One of the first individuals arrested under the Selective Service Act of 1917, he received a sentence of one year and eight months in the Atlanta Federal Penitentiary for interfering with the draft. He described himself as “a man without a country,” an anarchist, and “an advocate of peace and not of force.” Deported on the Buford on January 21, 1919.

In Petrograd he secured factory employment but complained of poor conditions, prompting accusations that he was a “pampered bourgeois” nostalgic for “capitalist America.” After a decade of silence, he sent a coded letter to Alexander Berkman in 1931.

profiles.finding: Yale Harry Weinberger MS553 files corroborate 1917-19 anarchist detention/deportation; WWII serviceman and modern TXOne employee rejected. No verified portrait found.

profiles.name: Pavel Melnikov
profiles.description:
Pavel Melnikov was born 1886 in Kiev, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Worked as a laborer. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Attended gymnasium until age eighteen and worked as a clerk before emigrating. 

Around 1918 he joined the URW and became a national organizer and lecturer based in Seattle and San Francisco; he also taught English in the URW school in San Francisco. He was accused, without evidence, of involvement in bomb and assassination plots. Arrested April 23, 1917 in Trenton, New Jersey for allegedly making seditious remarks and again in March 1919 in San Francisco for vagrancy, he was deported on the Buford on December 21, 1919.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.finding: Commons Pavel Ivanovich Melnikov is the 19th-century writer, not 1886-born URW deportee; namesake rejected.

profiles.name: Peter Paich
profiles.description:
Peter Paich was born 1897 in Požega, Austria-Hungary (present-day Croatia). Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Joined the Socialist Party in Detroit in 1915 and the Workers’ International Industrial Union in Lorain, Ohio in 1918. Arrested August 1917 for distributing socialist literature and jailed four days. Arrested again April 1918 for distributing socialist and anti-conscription literature, then interned at Fort Oglethorpe as an “alien enemy.” Detained for deportation upon release in September 1919 and deported May 8, 1920 on the charge of being “likely to become a public charge,” as Socialist Party membership did not meet the legal definition of anarchism.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Samuel Miller
profiles.description:
Samuel Miller was born 1897 in Kiev, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Worked as a laborer. Immigrated to the United States in 1914.

An employee of Sears, Roebuck and Company in Chicago, as well as an IWW member and anarchist, Miller was arrested in July 1917. When asked his nationality, he replied: “I am international.” His attorney, Clarence Darrow, unsuccessfully argued that as a pacifist “philosophical anarchist” Miller should not fall under the anarchist exclusion laws. Deported December 23, 1920.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: W. Theo. Woodward
profiles.description: W. Theo. Woodward was listed in the National Civil Liberties Bureau's March 1919 compilation "War-Time Prosecutions and Mob Violence" among people convicted and jailed under World War I–era free-speech statutes — chiefly the Espionage Act, the Sedition Act, draft-obstruction charges, or wartime state and local laws. Per that record, on January 10, 1917 in Atlantic, Iowa, he was sentenced: 6 months and $600 for belonging to the People's Council, a violation of a state law. Prison sentence suspended. The NCLB — the direct predecessor of the American Civil Liberties Union — compiled these cases from April 1, 1917 to March 1, 1919 as a public record of the wartime suppression of free speech, a free press, and peaceful assembly.

profiles.name: Zys Korostyshevsky
profiles.description:
Zys Korostyshevsky was born 1897 in Radomyshl, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Worked as a garment worker. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Became a Tolstoyan anarchist in the US, embracing pacifism and agrarian ideals. Arrested in Chicago in June 1917, but the deportation warrant was canceled for lack of evidence. Arrested again in January 1919, he was ultimately deported on March 12, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.
